title: Maximum Number of Matching Indices After Right Shifts
statement:
`nums1` and `nums2` are integer arrays of the same length `n`. A **right shift** of `nums1` moves every element one place to the right, with the last element wrapping around to the front: the element at index `i` moves to index `(i + 1) % n`.

You may right-shift `nums1` any number of times, including zero. Afterwards an index `i` is **matching** when `nums1[i] == nums2[i]`. Return the largest number of matching indices you can reach.
notes:
## Intuition

Shifting `nums1` right `n` times brings it back to where it started, so only `n` different arrangements exist. With `n` at most 3000, trying every one of them and counting its matches takes about 9 million comparisons, which is quick. No rotated copy is needed either: after `shift` right shifts, index `i` holds the value that started at index `(i - shift) mod n`.

## Approach

1. Start with `best = 0`.
2. For every `shift` from `0` to `n - 1`, count `matches`: the indices `i` where `nums1[(i - shift + n) % n]` equals `nums2[i]`.
3. Keep the largest count in `best` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums1 = [3,1,2,3,1,2]`, `nums2 = [1,2,3,1,2,3]`.

- `shift = 0` compares `[3,1,2,3,1,2]` with `nums2`: 0 matches.
- `shift = 1` reads `nums1` as `[2,3,1,2,3,1]`: 0 matches.
- `shift = 2` reads it as `[1,2,3,1,2,3]`: all 6 indices match, so `best = 6`.
- Shifts 3, 4 and 5 give 0, 0 and 6 again, so the answer is `6`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): `n` shifts, each checked in O(n).
- Space: O(1): the shifted array is only read through the index formula, never built.

## Pitfalls

- Add `n` before taking `% n`: in JavaScript `-1 % 6` is `-1`, not `5`.
- Matching is about positions after one common shift. Counting values the arrays share, or letting each index pick its own shift, overcounts.
- `shift` only needs to go up to `n - 1`; a shift of `n` is the same as no shift.
- The answer can be `0`, for example when the arrays share no value.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of both arrays |
| `best` | most matches seen so far |
| `shift` | how many right shifts are applied to `nums1` |
| `matches` | matching indices for the current shift |
| `i` | index of `nums2` being compared |

narration.3: No arrangement has been tried yet, so the best count is 0.
narration.4: Try every number of right shifts; n shifts would bring nums1 back to the start.
narration.5: Count the matching indices for this shift from zero.
narration.7: After shift right shifts, index i holds the value that started at (i - shift) mod n.
narration.8: Equal values: one more matching index.
narration.11: Keep the best count over all shifts tried so far.
narration.13: The largest number of matching indices over every shift.
